[Elementary Statistics](../index.qmd) / Describing distributions

## Why can one observation change a summary?

Imagine 10 people completing a short attention task. Most finish in about 8 to 14 minutes. If one person takes considerably longer, how should we describe a typical completion time?

We will explore **center** (mean and median), **spread** (sample standard deviation and range), and **z-scores** using a small simulated dataset. This lesson supports topics from Weeks 3 and 4 of the proposed course. Other topics in those weeks, including graph interpretation and introductory scatterplots, will have separate resources.

::: {.clt-overview}

**Learning goals**

After this activity, you should be able to:

1. Explain the difference between the mean and median.
2. Predict how an unusually large observation affects measures of center.
3. Interpret sample standard deviation as a measure of variability.
4. Explain what a z-score tells us about an observation's position relative to the mean.

**Before starting:** Review how to order numerical values and calculate an average.

:::

## Make a prediction

The data below represent **simulated task-completion times**, not observations from real students or patients. You can change only the final person's time. The other nine times stay fixed.

Which measure will change more if the final time increases from **14 to 35 minutes**, the mean or the median? Make a prediction, then experiment.

## Interpret what you find

First select **Original time: 14**, then **Unusually high: 35**. Compare how much the mean, median, standard deviation, and range change. Notice that the same ten people are represented in both versions; only one value changes.

## What do these summaries tell us?

The **mean** is the sum of the observations divided by their number. The **median** is the middle value after sorting (or the average of the two middle values for an even number of observations). Both describe center, but they respond differently to an extreme value.

The **sample standard deviation** describes variability around the sample mean, in the same units as the observations. A **z-score** expresses a value's distance from the mean in standard-deviation units: $z=(x-\bar{x})/s$.

**Why this makes sense:** An unusually long completion time pulls the mean upward because the mean includes every value. The median is based on which observations occupy the middle positions, so it may barely change. The unusually high time also makes the observations more spread out. A z-score puts an individual time in context by asking how far it sits from the current average relative to that spread.

An unusual value is not necessarily a mistake. Investigate its source and context before deciding how to report or handle it.
